Abyssal Corrosion Syndrome (also: Abyss Corrosion Syndrome, Draught of Lucidity): Abyssal Corrosion Syndrome is an illness caused by direct contact with high concentrations of Abyssal power. It harms body and mind, can leave irreversible mental trauma, and mostly appears as hallucinations. It is named in Natlan during the Abyssal invasion. The worst cases are treated with the Draught of Lucidity.

In universe: Symptoms include psychosis, often with sight and sound hallucinations and the reliving of past traumas. Severity follows the patient's level of trauma. In "For the Same Land," Atoco relives a childhood near-drowning, and Cochitta's fear of losing her loved ones is triggered by the memory of her parents' deaths.

Treatment: Verbal and physical contact for light cases; the Draught of Lucidity for severe ones.

1.content:
Adeptal Arts (also: Adeptus Arts, adeptal power, adeptal energy, arts of the adepti, adeptal techniques): The Adeptal Arts are the techniques of Liyue's adepti, the illuminated beasts and gods led by Rex Lapis (Morax). They include alchemy for making elixirs, paper sigils that store adeptal power, the creation of pocket-world abodes, and dream arts. The power is generally harmful or lethal to ordinary mortals, and the adepti guard their methods closely.

In universe: Adepti can manipulate elemental energy without a Vision, which is why Liyue's people call them the "three-eyed" mighty and illuminated adepti; their Visions, when worn, are shown as a human convention. Beyond that, each adeptus carries adeptal energy with an effect particular to them, which is dangerous to mortals who spend too long near it.

Limits: Adeptal power harms mortals and is not given freely. Humans can learn some adeptal arts, but they do not become adepti, since canon applies the word to non-humans (half-humans can qualify).

2.content:
Aggravate (also: Aggravate reaction, Electro Catalyze reaction): Aggravate is the Electro half of the Catalyze family. First an Electro hit and a Dendro hit meet and put a Quicken aura on the target; after that, further Electro hits on the Quickened target trigger Aggravate, which makes each of them hit harder by a flat amount. It is a combat rule rather than a story event, and the reaction arrived with Version 3.0.

In universe: Canon presents Aggravate only through the Elemental Trial tutorial and gameplay text. The wiki records that the Electro and Dendro reaction is said to have a deep connection to the history of Sumeru, but no source read for this entry explains how.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): an Electro attack on a target with a Quicken aura triggers Aggravate and adds an Additive Base DMG Bonus to that attack's damage. Aggravate does not consume the aura.

Limits: Aggravate needs an existing Quicken aura and an Electro attack that can apply Electro; Dendro attacks trigger Spread instead.

3.content:
Alchemy (also: alchemist arts, Bio-Alchemy, biological alchemy): Alchemy in Teyvat is the art of transmuting and combining matter. In its everyday form it mends, brews and refines; at its peak it can reshape living things, even create them. Mondstadt practises it openly (the Knights of Favonius employ a Chief Alchemist, Albedo), Sumeru's Akademiya studies it in its Spantamad Darshan, Liyue's adepti keep a private version, and Snezhnaya forbids it. The pinnacle is Khaenri'ah's Art of Khemia, which creates life and is tied to the Cataclysm.

In universe: Alchemy is a body of techniques for transforming materials and living things by controlled processes: potions, solutions, transmutation arrays, cauldrons. It does not require a Vision; Sucrose received hers in the middle of an alchemy experiment, not before it. Alchemy comes in levels: ordinary alchemy is limited, while the deepest forms touch the nature of life itself.

Mondstadt: Mondstadt practises alchemy openly. The Knights of Favonius count a Chief Alchemist among their ranks; Albedo holds that post, with Sucrose and Timaeus as his assistants. Sucrose practises bio-alchemy, working to modify existing life.

4.content:
Anemo (also: Anemo element, element of wind): Anemo is the element of wind, one of Teyvat's seven elements. Its Archon is Barbatos, who lives in Mondstadt as the bard Venti; Mondstadt is the nation of wind and freedom. People with Anemo Visions raise gusts and updrafts, pull or push things with vortices, and glide on the wind. The Anemo Dragon Sovereign is Dvalin, once called Stormterror. The Harbinger Signora took the Anemo Gnosis from Venti for the Tsaritsa.

In universe: Most people cannot use Anemo. Those who can usually hold an Anemo Vision. Venti draws on the Anemo Authority of his divine throne in Celestia instead; the "Vision" on his hip is, in his words, "a glowing glass ball I carry around to avoid suspicion."

Archon and nation: Archon: Barbatos (Venti), the God of Freedom, who with Morax is one of the two surviving original members of The Seven. Nation: Mondstadt, which he deliberately leaves to govern itself.

Elemental beings: Dvalin, the Anemo Dragon Sovereign, and Anemo elemental lifeforms such as slimes, specters and the Anemo Hypostasis.

Known uses: Gusts and updrafts, gliding, whirlwinds that gather foes or debris, and pushing things away. Anemo also scatters other elements.

Limits: Anemo does not react with Geo or Dendro.

Interactions: Swirl: when Anemo meets Pyro, Hydro, Electro or Cryo it spreads that element to nearby targets (own entry).

5.content:
Archaeolune Energy (also: Archaeolune, ancient moon energy, ancient moon's power, Blue Kuuvahki, Moonvein Suffusion, Archaeolune Ripples): Archaeolune Energy is an ancient, primordial power found on the Frost Moon, the one intact moon above Nod-Krai. It is closely tied to kuuvahki, the moonlight-power of Nod-Krai, and is considered kuuvahki's primordial form; characters in the story usually call it "ancient moon energy". It fills the moon's core, powers the dragon-built machines on the moon, and can create life. It first appeared in the Moon Gazing quests (Version 6.7).

In universe: Kuuvahki, the power of the Three Moons, is a primordial form of elemental energy that belongs to the Light Realm. Columbina says kuuvahki and the ancient moon's energy are both, in essence, the power of the Light Realm. The wiki describes Archaeolune Energy as the primordial form of kuuvahki that shares the properties of two other primordial energies: phlogiston (programmable matter, an energy source, and a medium for storing and recording information) and the Primordial Sea (the power of creation, including the creation of life).

6.content:
Arkhe (also: Pneuma, Ousia, Pneumousia, Pneuma and Ousia, Pneuma-Ousia Annihilation, Arkhe alignment): Arkhe is a pair of opposing energies native to Fontaine: Pneuma and Ousia. When one meets the other, the two annihilate and release a greater burst of energy. This Pneuma-Ousia Annihilation is what powers most of Fontaine's Clockwork Meka. Arkhe is not one of the seven elements. It is a separate, Fontaine-specific energy, and most Fontainian characters carry one alignment of it.

In universe: In-game tutorials describe Pneuma and Ousia as properties found in the life-forms, earth, air and watery veins of Fontaine. When energies of different properties collide they annihilate and yield greater energy. This is the principle that powers many Clockwork Meka.

Known uses: Disabling Clockwork Meka by striking with the opposite alignment, solving Fontaine puzzles, and stunning Breacher Primuses in their stressed state.

Limits: Arkhe is not an element and does not react like one.

7.content:
Arkhium (also: Arkhium crystal, Arkhium ore, Arkhium Kinetic Core, Arkhium Stock, Arkhium Lumenite): Arkhium is a yellow, green and blue crystalline ore that occurs in parts of Fontaine and works as an extremely potent energy source. The Fontaine Research Institute tried to use it to counter gravity so that a "city in the sky" could ride out the prophesied flood. A mechanical malfunction overloaded the Arkhium Kinetic Core, and the explosion destroyed much of the old Institute grounds.

Properties: Arkhium separates matter, or certain things outside of matter, according to archive text; the separation can apparently be reversed, though there has been little interest in doing so. It is either inert, stable and giving off no energy, or activated, unstable and emitting powerful pulses.

Limits: Arkhium is not a Vision element, and not the same thing as Arkhe.

8.content:
Art of Khemia (also: The Art of Khemia, Khaenri'ahn alchemy, Khemia): The Art of Khemia is the alchemy of Khaenri'ah. Because Khaenri'ah was an underground nation with little natural fauna, its alchemy centred on creating life, and it is quite different from the alchemy practised in the Seven Nations. Its master was "Gold" Rhinedottir, who made the dragon Durin, the synthetic human Albedo and many monsters. The Art played a major role in the fall of Khaenri'ah in the Cataclysm 500 years ago.

In universe: Khemia sits at the far end of alchemy: those who combine the pinnacle of alchemical skill with vast learning can create synthetic life, which Albedo calls the "apex achievement". Canon names only Rhinedottir as having reached that level. Its inner workings and history are not explained in canon.

Known creations: Durin (dragon), Albedo (synthetic human), the riftwolves, Elynas, the Bakunawa, Sebas and the False Horned Steed.

9.content:
Ascension Phase (also: character ascension, weapon ascension, ascending a character): Ascension Phase is a game-mechanics term: the number of times a character or weapon has been ascended. It determines the maximum level the character or weapon can reach; the highest phase, 6, allows level 90. It is not something characters experience in the story.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): ascending raises the level cap. Characters need level-up materials, enhancement materials and local specialties; weapons need weapon ascension materials and enhancement materials.

Limits: Applies to playable characters and weapons only; it has no canonical in-world explanation.

10.content:
Azosite (also: Azosite energy, Azosite system, Azosite-powered system, Azosite smelting): Azosite is an ancient form of energy used by the Khaenri'ahns. It was made by extracting pure elemental energy from ley lines and smelting it into solid Energy Blocks, and it powered everything from ordinary ruin machines to large weapons-testing facilities. Over time the Khaenri'ahns found more effective sources, such as Abyssal energy, which gradually replaced it.

In universe: The Khaenri'ahns refined elemental energy out of the ley lines and processed it into Energy Blocks. Azosite is not a separate force: notes found in the ruins say it is not fundamentally different from elemental energy and cannot break the rules that elemental energy must follow.

11.content:
Bloom (also: Bloom reaction, Dendro Core, Dendro Cores, Bountiful Core, Bountiful Cores): Bloom is what happens when Dendro and Hydro meet on a target, in either order. The result is a Dendro Core: a small bud-like object that sits on the field for a few seconds and then bursts in a spray of Dendro damage around it. It arrived in Version 3.0 with the Dendro element.

In universe: Canon offers no in-world explanation. Bloom is shown in tutorials and combat, not discussed by characters in the sources read. Treat it as a gameplay abstraction: a scene may borrow its look (a seed forming from water and verdant energy) but should not present a named in-world law.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Dendro applied to a Hydro-affected target, or Hydro applied to a Dendro-affected one, creates a Dendro Core. It lasts up to 6 seconds. If it expires while the character who made it is still in the party and alive, it explodes for area Dendro damage in a 5 m radius, hurting enemies and players alike. Otherwise it simply disappears.

12.content:
Bond of Life (also: Life Bond): Bond of Life is a combat mechanic that prevents healing. Some enemy, weapon or talent effects place it on a character; while it lasts it soaks up incoming healing instead of restoring health. It is a gameplay abstraction, not a story concept.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): while Bond of Life is active, healing the character is absorbed by the bond according to its value rather than restoring HP. It clears once healing equal to its value has been taken in, or when the player visits a Statue of The Seven.

Limits: No in-world account exists; keep it to a combat effect.

13.content:
Burgeon (also: Burgeon reaction, Pyro Bloom reaction, Pyro-Dendro Core reaction): Burgeon is a Dendro elemental reaction. A Dendro Core (the seed-like orb a Bloom leaves behind) that is struck by Pyro explodes immediately, in a bigger burst of Dendro damage than the core would deal on its own. It is one of the two ways to cash in a Bloom early, the other being Hyperbloom.

In universe: Canon gives no in-world explanation for Burgeon. The pages read treat it purely as a combat rule, so it is best understood as what fire does to a ripe seed of plant energy.

Gameplay: Gameplay: when Pyro is applied to a Dendro Core, Burgeon triggers. It uses up the core and deals Dendro area damage, wider and heavier than an unaided core burst.

Limits: Burgeon needs a Dendro Core, so it needs Bloom first. It does nothing to a Bountiful Core.

14.content:
Burning (also: Burning reaction, Burning aura): Burning is what happens when Pyro and Dendro meet on a target, in either order. It sets the target alight: fire damage over time, a small burst of flame around them, and a flaming aura that lasts while the Dendro on the target lasts. Plants and grass catch fire the same way.

In universe: Canon offers no in-world explanation. Burning appears in tutorials and combat, not in character dialogue in the sources read. Treat it as a gameplay abstraction that a scene may borrow from.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): applying Pyro to a Dendro-affected target, or Dendro to a Pyro-affected one, triggers Burning. It deals area Pyro damage and applies 1 gauge unit of Pyro within a 1 m radius to players and enemies, with a 2 second internal cooldown on that Pyro application. The Burning aura looks like an animated Pyro aura and coexists with the underlying Pyro and Dendro auras.

15.content:
Constellation (also: Constellations, Stella Fortuna, star sign, constellation level): "Constellation" means two linked things in Teyvat. In lore, the stars of a constellation stand for a person's fate, and the Heavenly Principles are said to pull those stars like strings on the people of the mortal world. In gameplay, each playable character has six Constellation levels, upgrades unlocked one at a time with that character's Stella Fortuna.

In universe: The stars of Teyvat are tied to Fate. Constellations are an extension of that idea: patterns of Stella Fortuna that trace what a person will be, and strings by which the Heavenly Principles direct mortals.

16.content:
Cryo (also: Cryo element, element of ice, element of frost): Cryo is the element of ice and frost, one of Teyvat's seven elements. Its Archon is Anastasya, the Tsaritsa (divine name Vassaga), God of Love, who rules Snezhnaya, the land of eternal winter. Cryo users chill, freeze and slow their enemies. The Tsaritsa also holds the Cryo Gnosis and, as of 7.1, five of the other six.

In universe: Most people cannot use Cryo. Those who can usually hold a Cryo Vision, a crystal that grants control of the element. The Tsaritsa draws instead on the Cryo Authority of her divine throne in Celestia, and on her Gnosis.

Archon and nation: Archon: Anastasya Feodorovna Snezhnaya, the Tsaritsa of All Snezhnaya, Cryo Archon of the Seven and God of Love. Her divine name is Vassaga. Nation: Snezhnaya, which she governs directly from Zapolyarny Palace.

Elemental beings: Cryo Slimes, Specters, Cicins, Whopperflowers, Regisvines, Abyss Mages and the Cryo Hypostasis are Cryo creatures. The Cryo Dragon Sovereign is dead.

Known uses: Chilling and freezing foes, raising ice, and slowing movement.

Limits: Cryo does not react with Dendro.

Interactions: Cryo reacts with Electro (Superconduct), Hydro (Frozen), Pyro (Melt), Anemo (Swirl, and Stellar Swirl since 7.0) and Geo (Crystallize). Each has its own entry.

17.content:
Crystallize (also: Crystallize reaction, Crystallize shard, Crystallize shield, Elemental Shard): Crystallize is what happens when Geo hits a target already affected by Pyro, Hydro, Electro or Cryo. It deals no damage. It leaves a shard of that element, and a character who picks the shard up gains a shield of the same element.

In universe: Canon offers no in-world explanation. Crystallize shows up in tutorials and combat, not in character dialogue in the sources read. Treat it as a gameplay abstraction that a scene may borrow from.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): the shard (Electro, Pyro, Hydro or Cryo) lasts 15 seconds on the field, with a short delay before it can be picked up. Picking it up grants an elemental shield that also lasts 15 seconds. Enemies cannot pick shards up.

18.content:
Delusion (also: Delusions, Evil Eye, Fatui Delusion, counterfeit Vision): Delusions are Vision-like devices made by the Fatui. They let their wielders command an element, can be used by almost anyone, and are said to be far stronger than Visions. The price is the user's vitality: they can drain life force, age the wearer or backfire fatally. How they are made is secret; the evidence points to the remains of dead gods. The Chinese name means "Evil Eye", a counterpart to the "Eye of God".

In universe: A Delusion looks like a Vision with a Fatui emblem instead of an element symbol. It is a glass orb in a jagged frame, and its colour follows the element it grants. Unlike a Vision, which the gods give to one person, a Delusion can be used by anyone who holds it.

Side effects: Delusions drain the user's life force and can backfire. Resistance soldiers in Inazuma aged rapidly; Teppei died of it. Diluc's father Crepus was fatally hurt when one backfired.

19.content:
Dendro (also: Dendro element, element of plants, element of grass): Dendro is the element of plants and growth, one of Teyvat's seven elements. Its Archon is the God of Wisdom, whose divine name is Buer and who today is Lesser Lord Kusanali (Nahida); her nation is Sumeru, a land of rainforest and desert. Dendro Visions let their holders call up vines, leaves and seeds, and it is the element behind Quicken and Bloom reactions. The Dendro Dragon Sovereign is Apep, who once ruled all of Sumeru. Nahida traded her Dendro Gnosis to the Harbinger Dottore in Chapter III, and as of 7.1 the Tsaritsa holds six Gnoses.

In universe: Most people can only use Dendro through a Dendro Vision; Nahida draws on the Dendro Authority of her divine throne in Celestia. In Sumeru, Dendro is bound up with life, growth and dreams: the rainforest, its Aranara, and the Akasha network all trace back to the God of Wisdom.

Archon and nation: Archon: the God of Wisdom, divine name Buer. The current holder is Lesser Lord Kusanali (Nahida); before her it was Greater Lord Rukkhadevata. Nation: Sumeru, whose capital Sumeru City is built on the Divine Tree.

Elemental beings: Apep, the Dendro Dragon Sovereign, and Dendro elemental lifeforms such as slimes, specters and the Dendro Hypostasis.

Known uses: Vines, leaves, seeds and plants grown or controlled, and Dendro Cores from Bloom. Some Dendro enemies, such as Large Dendro Slimes, inflict a poison status.

Limits: Dendro does not react with Anemo or Geo.

Interactions: Quicken (Dendro + Electro) leads to Aggravate and Spread. Bloom (Dendro + Hydro) creates a Dendro Core, which can become Hyperbloom with Electro or Burgeon with Pyro. Burning (Dendro + Pyro) ignites. Each is its own entry.

20.content:
Diving (also: underwater exploration, Transoceanic Sourcewater, Fontaine's Blessing, Aquatic Stamina): Diving is how the Traveler explores underwater in Fontaine. Fontaine's lakes can be dived in once the first Statue of The Seven there is activated; a power called the Transoceanic Sourcewater keeps Vision holders, the Traveler and Paimon from drowning and lets them breathe and speak underwater. Ordinary people without Visions need diving gear and training. Fontaine is the only nation where diving is a game mechanic.

In universe: The tutorial calls the power the "Transoceanic Sourcewater" and says it flows out from a Statue of The Seven to bless those moving through Fontaine's lakes. In the text of the world, it lets Vision holders (and certain others, such as the Traveler and Paimon) breathe and speak underwater.

Limits: Diving is a Fontaine mechanic and does not apply in other nations.

21.content:
Eitr (also: Embryonic-Ichoric-Telluric-Rudiment, the Eitr): The Eitr, full name Embryonic-Ichoric-Telluric-Rudiment, is a forbidden creation of Hyperborea, the lost golden city of Snezhnaya. It contains the power of the Light Realm and can be used to alter living bodies. In 7.1 the dying Ronova fused an orb of it to Snezhnaya's Celestial Nail.

In universe: Canon describes the Eitr as the final result of forbidden technology that let Hyperborea's master crafters modify the very essence of life. It carries Light Realm power. Used on a body, it can give a creature power beyond what its kind normally has.

22.content:
Electro (also: Electro element, element of lightning): Electro is the element of lightning, one of Teyvat's seven elements. Its Archon is Beelzebul, publicly the Raiden Shogun, the God of Eternity who rules Inazuma, the land of thunder. Electro Vision holders conjure sparks, bolts and charged storms, and Electro reacts with every other element but itself. As of 7.1 the Electro Gnosis is no longer with the Archon: it passed through several hands and now belongs to the Tsaritsa.

In universe: Most people cannot use Electro. Those who can usually hold an Electro Vision. The current Electro Archon, Ei, draws on the Electro Authority of her divine throne in Celestia; she no longer holds the Electro Gnosis.

Archon and nation: Archon: Ei, whose divine name is Beelzebul, the God of Eternity, publicly known as the Raiden Shogun. "Baal", the divine name of her late twin Makoto, and the title Raiden Shogun were long understood to refer to both twins. Nation: Inazuma, ruled by the Inazuma Shogunate.

Elemental beings: Electro elemental lifeforms such as Electro Slimes, Electro Specters and the Electro Hypostasis, and the Thunder Manifestation of Amakumo Peak.

Known uses: Lightning strikes, sparks that chain between foes, charged fields, and fast bursts of speed. Electro also sets off reactions with Pyro, Hydro, Cryo, Anemo, Geo and Dendro.

Limits: Electro does not react with itself. It has no effect of its own beyond enabling reactions.

Interactions: Overloaded (with Pyro) explodes. Superconduct (with Cryo) damages and weakens Physical resistance. Electro-Charged (with Hydro) damages over time. Swirl spreads Electro. Crystallize with Geo forms a shield-granting shard. Quicken with Dendro enables Aggravate and Spread.

23.content:
Electro-Charged (also: Electro-Charged reaction, Electrocharged, Electro Charged): Electro-Charged is what happens when Electro and Hydro meet on a target, in either order. The target keeps both Hydro and Electro on it and takes Electro damage once a second, and the shock jumps to another wet enemy nearby. It continues until one of the two elements is used up.

In universe: Canon offers no in-world explanation. Electro-Charged appears in tutorials and combat, not in character dialogue in the sources read. Treat it as a gameplay abstraction that a scene may borrow from.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Electro-Charged leaves the target with a Hydro aura and an Electro aura at the same time. It deals Electro damage once per second; each tick reduces both auras by 0.4 gauge units, and it ends when either aura is gone. Normal aura decay still applies.

24.content:
Elemental Burst (also: Ultimate, character ultimate): The Elemental Burst, or Burst, is a Talent that needs Energy and is usually stronger than the Elemental Skill. Fans call it the ultimate, or "Q" after its default PC key. Every character has one unlocked from the start. This is a gameplay mechanic; the narrative equivalent is a character unleashing their strongest technique.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): a Burst can be used when (1) it is off cooldown and (2) the character holds at least the Burst's Energy Cost. Energy beyond the cost is ignored. Using it spends all Energy and starts a short cooldown, though Energy can still be gathered during the cooldown.

Limits: The Energy meter, key binding and cooldown are interface concepts, not things characters mention.

25.content:
Elemental Mastery: Elemental Mastery is an attribute that enhances elemental reactions. The higher it is, the stronger the reactions a character triggers. It is a gameplay stat with no direct in-world number.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): on triggering a reaction, Elemental Mastery boosts it. Overloaded, Superconduct, Electro-Charged, Burning, Shattered, Swirl, Bloom, Hyperbloom, Burgeon, Lunar-Charged, Lunar-Bloom, Lunar-Crystallize and Stellar-Conduct deal more damage. Melt and Vaporize multiply the triggering attack. Aggravate and Spread add bonus base damage to the triggering attack. Crystallize shields absorb more damage.

Limits: No canon defines the stat outside the game's interface and tutorial text.

26.content:
Elemental Reaction (also: Elemental Reactions, elemental aura, Transformative Reaction, Amplifying Reaction, Additive Reaction): An Elemental Reaction happens when an element is applied to a target that already carries a different element. Attacks, Visions and elemental creatures leave an "aura" of their element on a target, and a second element meeting it triggers an effect such as Vaporize, Melt, Overloaded, Swirl, Bloom or Crystallize. It is chiefly a combat rule, so treat it as a gameplay abstraction that a scene may borrow from, not as a named in-world law.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): when an element is applied to an enemy, player or object it leaves an aura that fades over time. Applying a second, different element triggers a reaction, which consumes some or all of the first aura. Many attack sources have an internal cooldown, so they cannot reapply their element, or trigger a reaction, on every hit.

27.content:
Elemental Resonance (also: Team Bonus, party resonance): Elemental Resonance is a game bonus granted when a full party contains certain element combinations. Two or more characters of the same element among the first four party slots trigger that element's resonance. Four different elements trigger Protective Canopy. It is a gameplay mechanic, not an in-world phenomenon.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore), as of 7.1:
- Fervent Flames (two Pyro): 40% shorter Cryo effect, ATK +25%.
- Soothing Water (two Hydro): 40% shorter Pyro effect, Max HP +25%.
- High Voltage (two Electro): 40% shorter Hydro effect; certain Electro reactions have a 100% chance to produce an Electro particle (5 s cooldown).
- Shattering Ice (two Cryo): 40% shorter Electro effect, CRIT Rate +15% against Frozen or Cryo-affected enemies.
- Impetuous Winds (two Anemo): stamina use -15%, movement speed +10%, skill cooldowns -5%.
- Enduring Rock (two Geo): shield strength +15%, plus damage and Geo RES reduction effects when shields or Moondrifts are nearby.
- Sprawling Greenery (two Dendro): Elemental Mastery +50 and reaction-triggered boosts.
- Protective Canopy (four unique elements): all Elemental RES +15% and Physical RES +15%.

Limits: Only a full party triggers resonance, except that Protective Canopy needs four unique elements. Extra same-element characters add nothing.

28.content:
Elemental Sight (also: elemental trails, elemental traces): Elemental Sight is the ability to perceive the elements around you. Toggling it makes elemental traces visible, shows which nearby things are affected by an element and highlights what can be interacted with. In Teyvat it is bound up with owning a Vision, or at least having elemental sensitivity, which is rare but known.

In universe: Elemental traces, also called elemental trails, are left behind by almost anything elemental, from slimes to gods to the wind itself, and can also be left by elemental magic or Vision holders. Everyone knows they exist, but those without elemental affinity find them hard to sense.

Gameplay: Gameplay: Elemental Sight is toggled with a button beside the minimap (middle mouse button by default on PC). A white range indicator spreads from the active character; background objects turn dark and muted while interactable ones are highlighted.

29.content:
Elemental Skill (also: Skill): The Elemental Skill, or just Skill, is a Talent every playable character has from the start. It costs no Energy; instead it goes on cooldown after use. It deals Elemental DMG, never Physical, and usually produces elemental particles that recharge the party's Energy.

In universe: This is a gameplay category. In the world, the skill is simply what a character does with their element or training, such as a technique, a summoned construct or a stance. The game fixes one such signature move per character.

Gameplay: Gameplay: using the Skill starts a cooldown whose length differs per character and which cannot be used again until it ends. Cooldown can be shortened, reset or extended by Talents, Constellations and other effects.

30.content:
Element (also: the Elements, the seven Elements, seven elements, elemental power, elemental Authority, elemental Authorities): The Elements are Teyvat's seven forms of elemental power: Anemo (wind), Geo (earth), Electro (lightning), Dendro (plants), Hydro (water), Pyro (fire) and Cryo (ice). Each is bound to one Archon and that Archon's nation. Ordinary people wield an element through a Vision, a jewel-like focus granted to those with strong desires.

In universe: Each element pairs with one Archon and one nation. Canon does not explain why.

The seven elements: Anemo: Mondstadt, Barbatos (Venti). Geo: Liyue, Morax (Zhongli). Electro: Inazuma, the Raiden Shogun (Ei). Dendro: Sumeru, Nahida. Hydro: Fontaine, Focalors. Pyro: Natlan, Mavuika. Cryo: Snezhnaya, the Tsaritsa (Anastasya).

Reactions: When a second element is applied to a target already carrying one, the two can react, for example Vaporize (Pyro with Hydro), Melt (Pyro with Cryo), Overloaded (Pyro with Electro) or Swirl (Anemo spreading another element).

31.content:
Energy (also: Elemental Energy, Energy Recharge, elemental particles, elemental orbs): Energy is the resource a character spends on their Elemental Burst. It builds up from elemental particles and orbs, which drop when Elemental Skills hit enemies or when enemies lose HP, and which recharge the whole party. Using the Burst empties it.

In universe: Characters do not speak of Energy as a number. The nearest in-world idea is elemental energy: pulses of an element a fighter gathers and then releases in a signature technique. Canon lore elsewhere says elemental energy was made by the Heavenly Principles, who divided raw currents of the Light Realm into seven using Phlogiston as a base (revealed 5.1).

Gameplay: Gameplay: each Burst has its own Energy cost, and a character cannot hold more than their base Burst needs. Being knocked out removes all of a character's Energy; if the active character falls out of bounds or drowns, the whole team loses all Energy.

32.content:
Exorcism (also: exorcist arts, Liyue thaumaturgy, thaumaturgy, thaumaturge, thaumaturges): Exorcists, also called thaumaturges, are Liyue people who have sworn an oath to cleanse the land of ghosts, spirits and demons. They are skilled in combat, magic and martial arts, and most come from families that keep exorcism as the family trade.

In universe: Chongyun's clan motto, as recorded in his and Shenhe's voice-overs, is to keep the heart pure and evil erased. The Tianheng clan keeps handed-down books recording the spirits it has defeated.

33.content:
Fetor (also: fetor of death, Fetor Node, death energy): Fetor is the energy that leaks into the living world when the border between life and death is disturbed. It is a sign of death pressing in on the living and harms those it touches. It was revealed in the limited-time Liyue event "Springtime Charms" (Lantern Rite, 5.3).

In universe: Small leaks happen whenever the border is disturbed. The Wangsheng Funeral Parlor is responsible for burning them away with its secret technique, the Art of Homa. In the event, Chongyun senses a strange chill around a dying elder and names it the "fetor of death."

34.content:
Frozen (also: Frozen reaction, Freeze Aura, Hydro-Cryo reaction): Frozen is the elemental reaction that happens when Hydro and Cryo meet on a target, in either order. It deals no damage by itself. It encases the target in ice and holds it immobile for a short time. A heavy blunt blow or a Geo attack can then break the ice open, which is the Shatter follow-up. It is a combat rule, so treat it as a gameplay abstraction that a scene may borrow from.

In universe: Canon does not give a story explanation for Frozen. The in-game text is a plain tutorial: when Cryo meets Hydro the Frozen reaction is triggered, and frozen beings cannot move.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Frozen needs Hydro applied to a target already carrying Cryo, or Cryo applied to a target carrying Hydro. It deals no damage of its own. It gives the target a Freeze Aura that immobilises it for a while.

Limits: Frozen does not hurt by itself, and it does not last long. It does not work on every enemy.

35.content:
Geo (also: Geo element, element of earth, element of rock, element of stone): Geo is the element of earth and stone, one of Teyvat's seven elements, seen in stone constructs, crystal shields and shaking ground. Its Archon is Morax (Rex Lapis), God of Contracts, patron of Liyue. He staged his own "death", gave up his Gnosis and now lives as Zhongli in Liyue Harbor.

In universe: Few people can use Geo, usually through a Geo Vision. Morax draws on the Geo Authority of his divine throne in Celestia instead; the Geo "Vision" at Zhongli's back is not a real one.

Archon and nation: Archon: Morax (Rex Lapis, Zhongli), oldest of The Seven. Nation: Liyue, now governed by humans.

Elemental beings: Azhdaha, the Geo Dragon Sovereign, sealed beneath the Dragon-Queller; Geo elemental lifeforms such as Geo Slimes, Geo Specters and the Geo Hypostasis; and the Geovishap line of dragons.

Known uses: Barriers and shields, summoned stone constructs, pillars of rock, shaking the ground, and petrifying or fixing a target in place.

Limits: Geo does not react with Anemo or Dendro; it crystallises Pyro, Hydro, Electro and Cryo.

Interactions: Crystallize: Geo meeting Pyro, Hydro, Electro or Cryo makes an elemental shard whose pickup gives a shield (own entry). Geo also gives Shatter, in which hitting a frozen target deals Physical damage and ends the freeze.

36.content:
Hexerei (also: Hexerei: Secret Rite, Hexerei character, Hexerei characters, Witch's Eve Rite): Hexerei (German for witchcraft) is a party Team Bonus introduced in Version 6.2. Certain characters become "Hexerei characters" by completing their Witch's Homework quests. Bring two or more into the party and the bonus Hexerei: Secret Rite activates, strengthening them.

Gameplay: Gameplay: finishing a character's Witch's Homework makes them a Hexerei character. With at least two Hexerei characters in the party, Hexerei: Secret Rite is active.

37.content:
Hydro (also: Hydro element, element of water): Hydro is the element of water, one of Teyvat's seven elements. Its homeland is Fontaine, the nation of justice. Two gods held the title of Hydro Archon, Egeria and then Focalors. Focalors executed herself in 4.2 and destroyed the Hydro Archon's divine throne, so Fontaine has had no Hydro Archon since. The Hydro Authority now belongs to Neuvillette, the reborn Hydro Dragon Sovereign.

In universe: Most people use Hydro through a Vision. Neuvillette needs none, because the Hydro Authority is his own. In how it interacts with other elements, rain, rivers, the sea and the Primordial Sea beneath Fontaine all count as Hydro.

Archon and nation: Hydro Archon: none as of 7.1. The divine throne was destroyed in 4.2. The two former Archons were Egeria and Focalors, both Gods of Justice among The Seven. Nation: Fontaine.

Elemental beings: Hydro Slimes, Hydro Samachurls, Hydro Specters, Hydro Mimics (summoned by Oceanids) and the Hydro Hypostasis. The Hydro Dragon Sovereign is Neuvillette.

Known uses: Currents, jets, bubbles, rain and tides, healing water, and soaking things so that they react to Electro and Cryo.

Limits: Hydro alone only soaks; it needs another element to do something special.

Interactions: Hydro reacts with Pyro (Vaporize), Cryo (Frozen), Electro (Electro-Charged), Anemo (Swirl), Geo (Crystallize) and Dendro (Bloom).

38.content:
Hyperbloom (also: Hyperbloom reaction, Electro Bloom reaction, Sprawling Shot): Hyperbloom is a Dendro elemental reaction. When Electro touches a Dendro Core (the orb a Bloom leaves behind), the core becomes a homing projectile, a Sprawling Shot, which flies to the closest enemy and bursts in a small area for strong Dendro damage. It is the Electro counterpart of Burgeon.

In universe: Canon gives no in-world explanation for Hyperbloom. The pages read treat it only as a combat rule, so it is best understood as a charged seed of plant energy flung at a foe.

Gameplay: Gameplay: when Electro is applied to a Dendro Core, Hyperbloom triggers. The core turns into a Sprawling Shot that homes in on the nearest enemy and deals Dendro area damage on impact.

Limits: Hyperbloom needs a Dendro Core, so it needs Bloom first. It does nothing to a Bountiful Core.

39.content:
Immortality and Resurrection (also: curse of immortality, Curse of Immortality, immortality in Teyvat, resurrection in Teyvat, Curse of Death, Elixir of Immortality): Teyvat has no single rule for avoiding death. Canon shows separate, bounded cases: the Curse of Immortality that Ronova, Ruler of Death, laid on pure-blooded Khaenri'ahns 500 years ago; long-lived adepti, gods and dragons, who still die or erode; zombies such as Qiqi; and Natlan's conditional Ode of Resurrection.

In universe: - Cursed immortality: pure-blooded Khaenri'ahns, by Ronova.
- Longevity: adepti, gods and dragons live for millennia but can die or be worn away.
- Zombification: adeptal energy (Qiqi) or an Elixir of Immortality (Jialiang).
- Resurrection: Natlan's Ode, for fallen Ancient Name bearers.

Limits: No source describes a way to undo the Curse of Immortality, and no resurrection is unconditional.

40.content:
Karma (also: karmic debt, divine karma, bad karma, karma of the yakshas): Karma, or karmic debt, is the corruptive residue left by the wills and powers of ancient gods slain in the Archon War. It seeps into land, monsters and people, and can drive humans mad. The yakshas were called by Rex Lapis to destroy it, and absorbed so much of it that most died or went insane. As of 7.1 the sole surviving yaksha, Xiao, still bears it.

In universe: During the Archon War, Morax subdued many gods. Their hatred and powers lingered in the world as half-awake remnants that corrupted land, spawned monsters and caused pestilence, miasma and mutations. Contact with karma can make humans insane and makes monsters stronger.

41.content:
Khvarena (also: Spirit Light, Khvarena of flowers, the Khvarena, Great Khvarena): Khvarena is a pure, divine energy of Sumeru. Nabu Malikata, the Goddess of Flowers, made it for one purpose: to oppose the cataclysm she foresaw. Its divine nature lets it purify Abyssal energy and Forbidden Knowledge. She called the first Khvarena her innocent, pure daughter and gave it to Greater Lord Rukkhadevata, who shaped it into the divine bird Simurgh. When the Abyss began to corrupt the Amrita, Simurgh shattered her form into countless motes of Khvarena. The only sentient ones became the Pari.

In universe: Khvarena is not presented as an element and is not tied to a Vision. It is an energy of divine life and purity, opposed to the darkness of the Abyss. It exists in many forms: wild motes in the Girdle of the Sands, the Pari, Plumes of Purifying Light and orbs of coalesced light that can raise barriers.

Known uses: Purifying: cleansing Abyssal energy and Forbidden Knowledge, and repairing seals against the Abyss. Raising barriers. Giving life to the Vourukasha Oasis.

Limits: Khvarena is not unlimited. Its sentient form, the Pari, lives out a fated duty and ends as a plume; the great form, Simurgh, gave up her shape. It cannot cleanse every taint: a Pari that is corrupted is rejected by the Oasis and becomes a tree.

42.content:
Kresnik Kristall (also: Kristall, Kresnik's Torch, Kresnik Torch, Kresnik Energy): Kresnik Kristall is the crystalline ore that keeps Snezhnaya warm. Burned in furnaces called Kresnik's Torches, it gives off heat efficiently, and every Snezhnayan city is built around one such torch. The ore is mined chiefly in Novokitezhgrad and shipped across the nation by rail.

In universe: Most Snezhnayan settlements need Kresnik Kristall to survive. Before the torches existed, the Eye of Graeae says, the land was made only of Frigid and Subzero Zones and unfit for human life.

43.content:
Lunar-Bloom (also: Lunar Bloom, Lunar-Bloom reaction, Verdant Dew): Lunar-Bloom is the Lunar Reaction between Dendro and Hydro, in either order. When the party includes a character whose Moonsign Benediction passive enables it, ordinary Bloom is replaced by Lunar-Bloom. By itself it does no damage. Instead it gives the party Verdant Dew, a stored resource certain characters spend to deal Lunar-Bloom damage, which can crit. It arrived in Version 6.0 (Luna I) with Nod-Krai.

In universe: Canon offers no in-world explanation. Verdant Dew and Lunar-Bloom are shown in tutorials and combat, not discussed by characters in the sources read. Treat them as a gameplay abstraction.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Lunar-Bloom does no damage on its own. The only ways to deal Lunar-Bloom damage are certain character talents and constellations, which spend Verdant Dew.

Limits: Lunar-Bloom does not deal damage when it triggers; the dew must be spent by a character that can use it.

44.content:
Lunar-Charged (also: Lunar Charged, Lunar-Charged reaction, thundercloud reaction): Lunar-Charged is the Lunar Reaction between Electro and Hydro. When the two meet on a target and the party includes a character whose Moonsign Benediction passive enables it, the usual Electro-Charged is replaced by Lunar-Charged. The reaction forms a thundercloud that keeps firing lightning at nearby enemies carrying both Electro and Hydro. Its damage can crit. It was the first Lunar Reaction, arriving in Version 5.8 alongside Ineffa.

In universe: Canon offers no in-world explanation. The thundercloud is shown only in tutorial and combat material. Treat it as a gameplay abstraction that a scene may borrow as a storm gathering over a fight.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): the thundercloud deals Electro damage to all Wet enemies who are also affected by Electro within roughly 5 m, every 2 seconds. A target that has not been hit in the last 2 seconds and is Wet or Electro-affected is struck at once when the other aura lands on it.

Limits: The cloud only strikes enemies that carry both Electro and Hydro (Wet), and only one cloud can exist at a time.

45.content:
Lunar-Crystallize (also: Lunar Crystallize, Lunar-Crystallize reaction, Moondrift Harmony): Lunar-Crystallize is the Lunar Reaction between Geo and Hydro. When the party includes a character whose Moonsign Benediction passive enables it, Hydro Crystallize is replaced by Lunar-Crystallize, which creates three Moondrifts around the target. Every third Lunar-Crystallize while Moondrifts are present sets them resonating in Moondrift Harmony, a tracking projectile that deals Geo damage and can crit. It arrived in Version 6.3 (Luna IV).

In universe: Canon offers no in-world explanation. Moondrifts and Moondrift Harmony appear in tutorial and combat material only. Treat them as a gameplay abstraction.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): triggering Lunar-Crystallize makes three Moondrifts near the target. While at least one is on the field, each third Lunar-Crystallize makes them resonate and fire a projectile that tracks the target for Geo damage.

Limits: Without a Moonsign Benediction character who enables it, Geo meeting Hydro is ordinary Hydro Crystallize.

46.content:
Lunar Reaction (also: Lunar Reactions, Lunar reaction family, Moonlight Reaction): Lunar Reactions are a family of three elemental reactions that appear when a party contains a character whose Moonsign Benediction passive allows them. Each one takes a normal Hydro-related reaction (Electro-Charged, Bloom, Crystallize) and replaces it with a Moon-themed version: Lunar-Charged, Lunar-Bloom and Lunar-Crystallize. Unlike their base versions, Lunar Reactions can land critical hits. They belong to the Nod-Krai era of the game.

In universe: Canon offers no in-world explanation. Lunar Reactions are presented as tutorial and combat material. Treat them as a gameplay abstraction: a scene may borrow the look (moonlit clouds, drifting stones, glowing dew) without naming an in-world law.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): while a character with a matching Moonsign Benediction is in the party, three Hydro-related reactions are replaced. Electro and Hydro give Lunar-Charged instead of Electro-Charged; Dendro and Hydro give Lunar-Bloom instead of Bloom; Geo and Hydro give Lunar-Crystallize instead of Hydro Crystallize.

Limits: Without a Moonsign Benediction character in the party, nothing changes and the ordinary reactions occur.

47.content:
Melt (also: Melt reaction, Melt DMG, Pyro-Cryo reaction): Melt is the elemental reaction between Pyro and Cryo. It deals no damage itself. Instead, the attack that triggers it hits harder. The bonus is larger when the trigger is Pyro landing on a target already affected by Cryo, and smaller when Cryo lands on a Pyro-affected target. It is a combat rule, so treat it as a gameplay abstraction, not a named law of the world.

In universe: Canon gives no story explanation for Melt. The in-game tutorial only says that when Pyro meets Cryo, Melt occurs, and the triggering source of damage receives a bonus.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Melt happens when Pyro hits a target that already carries Cryo, or when Cryo hits a target that already carries Pyro. The triggering attack's damage is multiplied. Pyro as the trigger gives a 2x multiplier; Cryo as the trigger gives 1.5x.

Limits: Melt cannot happen without a first element in place, and it does nothing to a target with neither Pyro nor Cryo on it.

48.content:
Moon Wheel (also: Moon Wheels, Nod-Krai Vision): A Moon Wheel is a Vision-like gem associated with Nod-Krai and the Three Moons. It is "formed from the stuff of the soul" and lets its bearer manipulate the elements like a Vision does, but it draws on kuuvahki, an ancient and purer form of elemental power, instead of ordinary elemental energy. In Nod-Krai a Moon Wheel looks identical to a Vision.

In universe: Moon Wheels work like Visions in practice: the bearer wears the gem and channels one element. The difference is the energy behind it. Kuuvahki is described as a primordial form of elemental power, the power of the Three Moons.

49.content:
Moonsign (also: Moonsign Level, Nascent Gleam, Ascendant Gleam, Moonsign: Nascent Gleam, Moonsign: Ascendant Gleam, New Moon's Embrace): Moonsign is a Team Bonus that sits beside Elemental Resonance. Some characters, mostly from Nod-Krai, carry a Moonsign Benediction passive, and each one in the party raises the party's Moonsign Level by one. One Moonsign character gives Nascent Gleam; two or more give Ascendant Gleam, which strengthens those characters and rewards non-Moonsign teammates for their skills. It is a game system, not a thing characters talk about, and it is tied to the moon-themed power of Nod-Krai.

In universe: Canon never explains Moonsign inside the story. The only in-world frame is the one the game gives: Nod-Krai is where "the new moon rises", and the tutorial says there are other ways to raise a party's Moonsign Level there.

Mechanics: Gameplay (not literal lore): the party gets a Moonsign Level equal to the number of Moonsign characters in it. One gives the Nascent Gleam effect. Two or more give Ascendant Gleam, which also includes Nascent Gleam's effects.

50.content:
Moonsign Benediction Passive (also: Moonsign Benediction, Moonsign Benediction Passives, Benediction passive): A Moonsign Benediction passive is a Passive Talent carried by certain characters, mostly from Nod-Krai plus Zibai of Liyue. While its owner is in the party, the party's Moonsign Level rises by one. On Columbina and on Moon Wheel users, the passive also lets a base reaction turn into a Lunar Reaction. It is a game-mechanic label, not something characters discuss in the story.

Gameplay: Game mechanics, not lore. Every Benediction passive adds +1 Moonsign Level while its owner is in the party. Illuga, Jahoda and Aino have only this plain form.

51.content:
Mystic Arts in Teyvat (also: Mystic Arts, mystic arts of Teyvat, magic in Teyvat): "Mystic arts" is the wiki's umbrella for the magical, ritual and supernatural traditions of Teyvat that are not just a Vision's elemental power. Mondstadt has openly practised alchemy and astrology; Liyue has the adepti's arts, exorcism, the Art of Homa and the Qimen arts; Inazuma has kitsune and bake-danuki magic, onmyoudou and tengu arts; Sumeru has the Akasha, Akademiya alchemy and the Aranara's Ararakalari. A parallel circle of powerful mages, the Hexenzirkel, practises witchcraft (its own entry).

In universe: Magic is not limited to Vision-bearers: Yelan says her clan has practised it for generations, and kitsune, adepti, tengu and aranara work wonders without Visions. Arts include divination, talismans, transformation, dream-magic, pocket dimensions, purification, alchemy and spirit-summoning.

Mondstadt: Alchemy is openly practised (bio-alchemy and Albedo's Art of Khemia). Astrology, including hydromancy, is practised by Barbeloth and Mona.

Liyue: The adepti's Adeptus Arts, taught to them by Rex Lapis (adeptal alchemy, dream-magic, talismans, pocket dimensions), plus exorcism, the Art of Homa and the Qimen arts.

Inazuma: Inazuma has the kitsune and bake-danuki's shapeshifting magic (Yae Miko is a master of kitsune spells), onmyoudou (paper shikigami and shikifuda, largely lost) and the tengu's feather-fan arts.

Sumeru: Sumeru has the Akasha knowledge system, Akademiya alchemy and the Aranara's memory-powered Ararakalari.

52.content:
Nightsoul's Blessing (also: Nightsouls, Nightsoul Burst, Nightsoul Transmission, Nightsoul Points, Nightsoul-aligned): Nightsoul's Blessing is the power state of Natlan's warriors. Natlan's dead enter the Night Kingdom, a realm of souls beneath the land; the souls there are called Nightsouls, and Natlanese fighters borrow their strength to run, climb, swim, leap and fight beyond what they could alone. The Wayob, spirits venerated by the six tribes, live in that realm, which the Lord of the Night made. It is a Natlan power tied to the land's own rules, not an element.

In universe: In story terms, the Night Kingdom is "a liminal space between the body and mind, life and death," deep underground. Natlanese people go there when they die and slowly lose themselves into a sea of souls. Living warriors can draw on those Nightsouls to enhance their abilities, which is Nightsoul's Blessing.

Known uses: Entering the state boosts mobility and fighting power; characters often move in ways ordinary people cannot. Kachina, for instance, rides Turbo Twirly while she has points left, and the state ends when they run out.

Limits: It is a Natlan power: it works best in Natlan and relies on the Night Kingdom's support.

Interactions: Phlogiston: Natlan's primordial energy, a form of Pyro, powers many Natlan devices and Saurian abilities, and is drawn on when Nightsoul points are gone.

53.content:
Overloaded (also: Overloaded reaction, Overloaded DMG, Pyro-Electro reaction): Overloaded is the elemental reaction between Pyro and Electro, in either order. It causes an explosion that deals area Pyro damage and throws nearby targets back. It is a combat rule, so treat it as a gameplay abstraction that a scene may borrow from, not a named law of the world.

In universe: Canon gives no story explanation for Overloaded. The in-game tutorial only says that when Pyro meets Electro, or Electro meets Pyro, Overloaded occurs, causing powerful explosions that deal area Pyro damage.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Overloaded happens when Electro hits a target carrying Pyro, or Pyro hits a target carrying Electro. The explosion deals area Pyro damage in a roughly 5 metre radius and causes strong knockback.

Limits: Overloaded needs both elements on the same target and does nothing to a target with only one. The knockback can scatter enemies instead of keeping them together.

54.content:
Party (also: Party Setup, party system, character switching, team composition): A party is a team of up to four playable characters. The player controls one at a time and can swap to another with a short delay. Team bonuses such as Elemental Resonance apply to the party as a whole.

In universe: Gameplay abstraction: in the story the Traveler travels with a handful of friends, but canon never states a four-person limit or an instant swap between them. Treat party swapping as the game's way of presenting who is fighting rather than a rule of the world.

Gameplay: Gameplay: switching characters has a 1-second cooldown. Up to four characters are deployed, added left to right, and a team with none cannot be deployed. Trial-character stages can add a fifth, the trial character, to a full party of four.

55.content:
Phlogiston (also: primal flame, Natlan Phlogiston, Liquid Phlogiston, Solid Phlogiston, Gaseous Phlogiston): Phlogiston is the primal energy of Natlan. People there can sense and use it: it powers machines, written signs and the Nightsoul's Blessing state of Natlan's warriors. It exists as liquid, solid and gaseous forms and flows along Spiritways. Canon calls it Teyvat's primordial energy and a form of "computronium", programmable matter that stores information. The dragon Kukulkan stole it and taught humans to use it.

In universe: In the world: Natlan's people use phlogiston for devices, signs, paints and warrior abilities. It carries heat and is dangerous to those who cannot handle it, but the Natlanese, nearly all of whom can use it, read it and work with it directly.

Forms: Gaseous, liquid and solid phlogiston, and Spiritways.

56.content:
Physical (also: Physical damage, Physical DMG, non-elemental damage): Physical is the eighth damage type in Genshin Impact: ordinary force with no element in it, such as a sword cut, a hammer blow or a crushing impact. The other seven damage types are the elements. Physical has no Archon, nation or Vision. It is a game category rather than a power the story names.

In universe: Canon never presents Physical as a force or Authority. In the story, a strike without elemental energy is just a strike: steel, muscle, teeth, claws or falling stone.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Sword, Claymore and Polearm attacks deal Physical DMG by default. So do Bow Normal Attacks and Aimed Shots that are not fully charged. Catalyst attacks are inherently elemental, so Catalyst users deal Physical DMG only through extra effects.

Limits: Physical does not react with any element and applies no aura.

57.content:
Prime Ice (also: Prime Ice Construct, Prime Ice Constructs, Prime Ice Resource, Fab-Vision): Prime Ice is a pale ice found across Snezhnaya that does not melt like ordinary frost. The Traveler can harvest it with the Fab-Vision function of the Eye of Graeae to gain Prime Ice Resource, then spend that resource, plus Kresnik Energy, to build Prime Ice Constructs: heat sources, grappling hooks, launch pads and more. Constructs can be taken down again for a refund of the ice.

In universe: In-world, Prime Ice is a durable ice native to Snezhnaya. The townsfolk of Svetloledovka make a living by harvesting it. Ordinary humans cannot shape it, but Snowland Fae can manipulate it naturally.

Limits: Prime Ice constructs can only be built in Snezhnaya using the Eye of Graeae. Each type has a limit per area, and the Traveler can only carry 400 units of resource.

58.content:
Pyro (also: Pyro element, element of fire, Pyro Archon's element): Pyro is the element of fire, one of Teyvat's seven elements. Its Archon is the God of War and bears the divine name Haborym; the current Pyro Archon is Mavuika, who rules Natlan, the land of Pyro. Unlike other Archons, Pyro Archons are mortals who win the throne in battle. People with Pyro Visions ignite, burn and explode things. The Pyro Gnosis never reached the Fatui; as of 7.1 it has vanished.

In universe: Most people use Pyro through a Vision. A Pyro Archon draws on the Sacred Flame and the Pyro Archon's divine throne instead. In Natlan the element is bound up with war, oaths and the idea that humans can become gods.

Archon and nation: Archon: the Pyro Archon, God of War among The Seven, divine name Haborym. Current holder: Mavuika. Nation: Natlan.

Elemental beings: Xiuhcoatl, the Pyro Dragon Sovereign, and Pyro lifeforms such as Pyro slimes, specters, Abyss Mages, the Pyro Hypostasis and the Pyro Regisvine.

Known uses: Igniting and burning things, explosions, heating, cooking and forging, and fire-based attacks. Pyro also melts ice and boils water in many fights.

Limits: Pyro does not react with Pyro. It does little on its own against water or ice.

Interactions: Vaporize with Hydro, Melt with Cryo, Overloaded with Electro, Burning with Dendro, Swirl with Anemo and Crystallize with Geo.

59.content:
Quicken (also: Quicken reaction, Quickened, Quicken Aura, Catalyze, Catalyze reactions, Dendro-Electro reaction): Quicken is the elemental reaction between Dendro and Electro, in either order. It deals no damage itself. It leaves the target Quickened, with a Quicken Aura that decays over time. While the aura lasts, further Dendro or Electro hits on the target trigger the Spread or Aggravate reactions, which add bonus damage to those hits. It is a combat rule, so treat it as a gameplay abstraction, not a named law of the world.

In universe: Canon gives no story explanation for Quicken. The in-game tutorial only says that when creatures are affected by Electro and Dendro, Quicken occurs and renders them Quickened, and that Quickened creatures hit by Electro or Dendro suffer additional damage through Aggravate or Spread.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Quicken happens when Dendro hits a target carrying Electro, or Electro hits a target carrying Dendro. It applies a Quicken Aura to the target, and the reaction itself deals no damage.

Limits: Quicken deals nothing by itself and needs both Dendro and Electro to be applied. It does not apply to plants that are not Dendro; "Wood" objects such as vines cannot trigger it.

60.content:
Physical laws and roleplay physics (also: roleplay physics, Teyvat physics, physical laws of Teyvat): This entry tells a narrator how physical reality works in Teyvat roleplay. The default is ordinary human biology and consequences: people eat, sleep, tire, are hurt and recover slowly, and death is permanent unless a specific canon mechanism applies. Visions, Archons, adepti and ancient powers are exceptions with limits. Game mechanics (health bars, respawning at a Statue of The Seven, instant fast travel) are abstractions, not literal in-world rules. Each section below separates what canon shows from this project's recommended reading.

Ordinary biology: Canon: ordinary people in Teyvat are shown living as humans do: they work, eat, rest and fall ill. Recommended: treat ordinary NPCs and Vision holders alike as physically human, with normal needs for food, water, sleep and shelter. A Vision grants control over one element, not toughness, immunity or freedom from need.

Death: Canon: death is real and usually permanent. Gods and Archons can die: Decarabian fell, Rukkhadevata and the Belyi Tsar died in past struggles against the Abyss, and Ronova died during the story. Recommended: a character who dies in a roleplay stays dead unless a canon mechanism below applies and the story earns it.

Resurrection: Canon shows only a few bounded forms: the Natlan Ode of Resurrection, adepti raising Qiqi as a zombie, and the cursed immortality of the Khaenri'ahns. None is a general fix for death.

61.content:
Saurian Indwelling (also: indwelling a Saurian, indwelt Saurian, Spiritsconce, Spiritsconces): Saurian Indwelling is an ability of the Traveler in Natlan: their spirit slips into a Saurian (one of Natlan's dragon-kin) and acts through its body, so they can run, climb, glide or swim as that creature does. The in-game tutorial credits "a mysterious power" with the gift. It is not presented as a Vision or an Archon's power, and almost nobody else in Natlan seems to know it exists.

In universe: Natlan's Saurians are descendants of Pyro vishaps that lost their ancient intelligence; they follow emotion and trust their human companions. Tribe members learn to read a Saurian's moods through long companionship. Indwelling is different: the Traveler's spirit enters the animal, and while inside, the speech of Saurians becomes understandable to them. Nobody is shown teaching the Traveler this; it simply works.

Limits: Some creatures refuse. A few quest-linked Saurians, such as "Half-Baked" in "Special Friends", reject the attempt with a message that a strong will refuses the indwelling. Indwelt Saurians are poor fighters and cannot dash to dodge attacks.

62.content:
Shattered (also: Shatter, Shattered reaction, Shatter reaction): Shatter, listed in the wiki's reaction list as Shattered, is the follow-up to Frozen. When a frozen target is hit by a blunt attack or a Geo attack, the ice breaks apart, the Freeze Aura is removed, and the target takes Physical damage.

In universe: Canon gives no in-world explanation for Shatter. The pages read treat it as a combat rule, so it is best understood as the ordinary physical fact that frozen things break when hit hard.

Gameplay: Gameplay: a Frozen target hit by a blunt attack (a claymore swing, a heavy hammer strike) or by Geo takes Shatter damage, and the Freeze Aura ends.

Limits: Shatter needs a Frozen target and a blunt or Geo hit. Weak physical strikes may not be enough.

63.content:
Shield (also: Shields, character shield, Crystallize shield): A shield is a barrier that takes damage in place of a character's HP. Characters gain them by collecting Crystallize shards or through certain talents, Constellations and weapons. Most are elemental and resist their own element especially well. Enemies have separate shields called wards.

In universe: In the world, shields appear as protective barriers: a wall of crystal or stone, a sheath of an element, or a bubble of energy. Characters do not speak of Shield Strength or absorption bonuses.

Gameplay: Gameplay: damage hits the shield's health first, and only the excess reaches the character. A shield that times out is destroyed, which can trigger effects such as Kachina's Constellation. If a character has several shields, one hit affects all of them at once.

64.content:
Souls (also: soul, the soul, afterlife, the dead in Teyvat, ghosts and spirits, soul-stuff): Canon has no single doctrine of the soul. The recurring picture: the soul is what outlasts the body. After death it is meant to return to the Ley Lines, or in Natlan to the Night Kingdom, where it eventually loses its sense of self. A soul or memory that fails to go can linger as a ghost. Older belief sent the noble dead to cities on the moons.

In universe: - Ley Lines: the standard destination. Ronova says that after the body dies the soul must return to the Ley Lines for death to be complete.
- Night Kingdom: in Natlan the dead go there; souls become Nightsouls and eventually merge into a sea of souls.
- Ghosts: souls or echoes that did not make the transition and linger on the surface.

Limits: No source describes how reincarnation works, and no source lets an ordinary person talk to or free a soul at will.

65.content:
Spiritway (also: Spiritways, Spiritdoor, Spiritdoors): Spiritways are pathways of constantly flowing Phlogiston in Natlan. Anyone who can ride one moves swiftly in the direction of the flow. They first appeared in Version 5.0.

In universe: In-game text describes a Spiritway as a pathway formed by flowing Phlogiston. Riding it carries the traveller along the flow.

66.content:
Spread (also: Spread reaction, Dendro Spread, Catalyze Spread): Spread is a Dendro elemental reaction. First, Dendro and Electro meet and make Quicken, which leaves a Quicken Aura on the target. Any later Dendro attack on that target then triggers Spread, which gives that attack a flat damage bonus. The Electro counterpart is Aggravate, and the Dendro bonus is the larger of the two.

In universe: Canon gives no in-world explanation for Spread. The pages read treat it as a combat rule, so it is best understood as plant energy riding on lingering charge and spreading through a target.

Gameplay: Gameplay: Dendro on a target with a Quicken Aura triggers Spread and adds a bonus to the attack that triggered it. Spread does not use up the Quicken Aura.

Limits: Spread needs a Quicken Aura first and only Dendro triggers it. It has no damage of its own.

67.content:
Stamina (also: Stamina bar, stamina meter, maximum stamina): Stamina is the yellow bar that drains when you sprint, dash, climb, swim, glide or make a charged attack. It is one pool shared by the whole party, starts at 100 and regenerates quickly when you stop.

In universe: Stamina is a game mechanic, not something characters mention by name. Gameplay abstraction: it represents the physical effort of running, climbing and swimming.

Gameplay: Gameplay: stamina is a shared party pool shown as a yellow bar beside the active character. It regenerates at 25 per second after 1.5 seconds of not spending it, and the bar hides itself when full. Switching characters does not restore it.

68.content:
Statue of The Seven (also: Statues of The Seven, Archon statue, Archon statues, Statue of Seven): Statues of The Seven are large stone statues of each nation's Archon, found across Teyvat. Legends say they were sculpted in the image of The Seven who sustain the world, and travellers pray to them for protection. In play they unlock the map, act as teleport waypoints, heal and revive the party, and swap the Traveler's element.

In universe: Mondstadt's statue honours the Anemo Archon, Liyue's the Geo Archon, Inazuma's the Electro Archon, Sumeru's the Dendro Archon, Fontaine's the Hydro Archon, Natlan's the Pyro Archon and Snezhnaya's the Cryo Archon. Each statue shows a hooded figure holding an object shaped like the region's Vision. The in-game map text calls them monumental statues that "watch over" the land.

Gameplay: Gameplay: each region's statues fill in map areas when first touched, unlock expeditions and teleport waypoints, revive fallen characters and heal the party. Interacting with a statue while playing the Traveler lets them change element to match that region.

69.content:
Stellar-Conduct (also: Stellar Conduct, Starlight Prism, Polestar Field): Stellar-Conduct is a Stellar Glimmer reaction from Snezhnaya. It happens when Cryo is applied to a target already affected by Electro, or the other way round, while a character with the matching Stellar Jubilee passive is in the party. It then replaces Superconduct. The reaction creates a Starlight Prism, which briefly turns the surrounding area into a Polestar Field.

In universe: Canon says nothing in-world about the prism or the field. The only lore note concerns the whole family: Stellar Glimmer reactions are said to have been introduced to ancient Snezhnaya by Saarelainen, the Third Descender, and the wiki cites a Version 7.0 livestream for that. Do not treat it as detailed history.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Stellar-Conduct does no damage by itself. Damage comes only from character talents and constellations, and may be Cryo or Electro depending on the source.

Limits: As of 7.1, no canon explains the reaction beyond its name and the family-level Saarelainen note.

70.content:
Stellar Glimmer Reaction (also: Stellar Glimmer, Stellar Glimmer Reactions): Stellar Glimmer reactions are a small family of Cryo-related elemental reactions tied to Snezhnaya. There are two: Stellar-Conduct (Cryo with Electro) and Stellar Swirl (Anemo with Cryo). They take the place of Superconduct and Cryo Swirl only when a character with a matching Stellar Jubilee passive is in the party, and those characters are Stellar Linchpin users from Snezhnaya, or the Cryo Traveler.

In universe: Canon gives the reactions almost no in-world explanation. The only lore note is that Stellar Glimmer reactions were introduced to ancient Snezhnaya by Saarelainen, the Third Descender. The wiki sources this to the Version 7.0 Special Program livestream rather than to quest text.

Limits: There are only two Stellar Glimmer reactions as of 7.1: Stellar-Conduct and Stellar Swirl. Do not invent further ones.

71.content:
Stellar Jubilee Passive (also: Stellar Jubilee, Stellar Jubilee Passives, Stellar Jubilee Passive Talent): A Stellar Jubilee Passive is a passive Talent held by characters with a Stellar Linchpin, plus the Cryo Traveler. It is what lets Stellar Glimmer reactions happen at all: with a holder in the party, the matching Cryo reactions turn into Snezhnayan Stellar Glimmer reactions. Sandrone, Odette and Vesna each have one, as does the Cryo Traveler.

Gameplay: Gameplay, not literal lore. With a holder in the party, a Superconduct triggered by any party member becomes Stellar-Conduct, and a Cryo Swirl becomes Stellar Swirl. The passive also raises the base damage of the converted reaction in proportion to the holder's ATK, and puts the holder into a "Radiance" state.

72.content:
Stellar Linchpin (also: Stellar Linchpins, Linchpin, Snezhnayan star-Vision): A Stellar Linchpin is a Vision-like object from Snezhnaya. Like a Vision, it lets its bearer channel elemental power, but Stellar Linchpin users often show a kind of power that seems to come from beyond Teyvat. The Fatui believe Linchpins are tied to the remains of the Third Descender, and they study them for their weapon against the Heavenly Principles (Project Mistilteinn). Known users are Sandrone (Cryo), Odette (Cryo), Vesna (Anemo), Danica (Electro) and Mitya (Electro). Linchpin bearers can enable the Stellar Glimmer reactions.

In universe: Visions are said to be a means of channelling elemental power for those who hold them. In Sandrone's explanation (as Marionette, in the 6.7 event), the same is true of Linchpins, with one difference: Linchpin users often exhibit a unique kind of power that seems to come from beyond Teyvat. What makes a Linchpin appear is not known.

Known users: Sandrone (Cryo), Odette (Cryo), Vesna (Anemo), Danica (Electro), Mitya (Electro).

73.content:
Stellar Swirl (also: Stellar Vortex): Stellar Swirl is a Stellar Glimmer reaction from Snezhnaya. It happens when Anemo is applied to a target already affected by Cryo, while a character with the matching Stellar Jubilee passive is in the party. It then replaces Cryo Swirl. It deals Anemo damage and leaves a Stellar Vortex that later bursts for Cryo damage.

In universe: Canon says nothing in-world about the vortex. The only lore note concerns the family: Stellar Glimmer reactions are said to have been introduced to ancient Snezhnaya by Saarelainen, the Third Descender, citing a 7.0 livestream.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): on triggering, one hit of Anemo damage is dealt to the target, and a Level 1 Stellar Vortex appears for 3 seconds. After a delay the vortex bursts, dealing area Cryo damage.

Limits: As of 7.1, no canon explains the reaction beyond its name and the family-level Saarelainen note.

74.content:
Superconduct (also: Superconduct reaction, Electro-Cryo reaction): Superconduct is the reaction that happens when Electro meets Cryo on a target, in either order. It is a burst of Cryo energy that damages everything in a small area and strips Physical resistance from the enemies it touches, so that sword, spear and fist hurt more for a while. It is a combat rule rather than a story event.

In universe: Canon does not explain Superconduct as a phenomenon of the world; it is introduced only through the game's Elemental Trial tutorial. Treat any in-world explanation as a scene decision, not as lore.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Superconduct deals AoE Cryo damage in a 5 m radius and reduces the Physical RES of enemies in the area by 40% for 12 seconds.

Limits: Superconduct needs both Electro and Cryo; no other element pair produces it.

75.content:
Swirl (also: Swirl reaction, Anemo Swirl, Pyro Swirl, Hydro Swirl, Electro Swirl, Cryo Swirl): Swirl is what happens when Anemo meets another element on a target: the wind catches that element and flings it outward, so everything nearby is hit or soaked with it. It works with Pyro, Hydro, Electro and Cryo, but not with Geo or Dendro. It is a combat rule rather than a story event.

In universe: Canon presents Swirl only through the Elemental Trial tutorial and gameplay text; no source read gives an in-world account of why wind spreads elements. Treat any explanation as a scene decision.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Swirl applies the non-Anemo element to targets within a 6 m radius, except the target the reaction was triggered on. Pyro, Electro and Cryo Swirl also deal AoE damage of that element; Hydro Swirl spreads Wet and deals damage only to the triggering target.

Limits: Swirl does not work with Geo or Dendro, and Anemo has no reaction with itself.

76.content:
Talent (also: Talents, character talents, Combat Talents, Passive Talents, Ascension Passive): "Talents" is the game's interface term for the abilities of a playable character. Most characters have three Combat Talents (Normal Attack, Elemental Skill, Elemental Burst), two Ascension Passives and one Utility Passive. It is a gameplay abstraction: in the story people simply use their powers, skills or arts. Never have a character say "my Talent level is 9".

In universe: Nothing found shows canon using "Talents" as an in-world category. What the interface lists as Talents are, in the story, a character's fighting style, Vision or Authority power, trained techniques and personal knacks.

Combat talents: Every character starts with three Combat Talents unlocked at level 1: the Normal Attack (their main attack form), the Elemental Skill (no Energy cost, but a cooldown) and the Elemental Burst (usually costs Energy).

Ascension passives: Two passive Talents unlock with Ascension: the 1st Ascension Passive (phase 1, character level 20) and the 4th Ascension Passive (phase 4). Most improve a Combat Talent.

Passive talents: Besides Ascension Passives, a character has a Utility Passive (also called an Exploration Talent), unlocked on acquisition; the Traveler has none. It does something outside combat: cooking, crafting or forging bonuses, reduced stamina cost, faster movement, expedition bonuses, resource markers on the map, or not startling certain wildlife.

Limits: Do not give a character a numeric Talent level, a cooldown readout or an Energy bar in dialogue, and do not call story powers "Talents".

77.content:
Teleport Waypoint (also: Teleport Waypoints, Portable Waypoint, Sub-Space Waypoint, fast travel): Teleport Waypoints are devices found across Teyvat. Once the Traveler unlocks one by touching it, it can be chosen on the map to fast travel there. In-world, they are old, odd structures the locals have grown used to without knowing what they are for; to the Traveler, a foreigner, their use is obvious.

In universe: Canon gives no explanation of who built Teleport Waypoints or how they work. Treat them as unexplained ancient machinery that happens to carry the Traveler between places.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Waypoints are map markers that are unlocked by interacting with them, then used to fast travel. Statues of The Seven, Statues of the New Moon, domains and High-Speed Transit Lanes also work as teleport points once unlocked.

78.content:
Vaporize (also: Vaporize reaction, Pyro-Hydro reaction): Vaporize is what happens when Pyro and Hydro meet on a target. It deals no damage by itself; instead the attack that triggers it hits much harder, as if the water flashed to steam under the blow. It is a combat rule rather than a story event.

In universe: Canon presents Vaporize only through the Elemental Trial tutorial and gameplay text. No source read for this entry gives an in-world account of why it amplifies damage, so any in-world explanation is a scene decision.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): Vaporize multiplies the damage of the triggering attack by 2 if Hydro is applied to a Pyro-affected target, and by 1.5 if Pyro is applied to a Hydro-affected target.

Limits: Vaporize needs both Pyro and Hydro, and it never creates damage on its own.

79.content:
Vision (also: Visions, God's Eye, Eye of God, allogene, allogenes): A Vision is a jeweled amulet, worn on the body, that lets its bearer channel one of the seven elements directly. The bearers are called allogenes: people with unusually strong desires or ambitions who might one day ascend to Celestia and become gods. Most people never receive one. A Vision does not give mastery, only the channel; the power still has to be practised.

In universe: A Vision links a person to an element (Pyro, Hydro, Anemo, Electro, Dendro, Cryo or Geo). Venti told the Traveler in the Prologue that Vision holders are allogenes who might ascend one day. A bearer has some elemental sensitivity and can sense their element more keenly than other people.

Allogenes: Allogene is the in-universe term for a person who is fit to hold a Vision. In the original Chinese, Japanese and Korean the word is the same as the game's title and means roughly "primordial god" or "original god". Allogenes may ascend to Celestia, though most do not.

Receiving: There is no sure way to get a Vision. They arrive during crises and fights, at moments of resolve or revelation, after major accomplishments, or on an otherwise ordinary day. Survival alone is not enough.

Masterless: When an allogene dies, their Vision goes dull, losing colour and power, and becomes a Masterless Vision. A Masterless Vision rarely resonates with someone new.

Related objects: Delusions, Gnoses, Moon Wheels and Stellar Linchpins are separate things; do not call them Visions.

80.content:
Witchcraft (also: witch magic, Hexenzirkel magic): Witchcraft in Teyvat is not a single taught discipline. The word points at the witches and mages of the Hexenzirkel, the circle of powerful women founded by the adventurer Alice, whose members practise astrology, alchemy and other arts, and at titles such as Lisa's "Witch of Purple Rose". Their powers are shown through individuals, from a near-omnipotent sorceress to members with no magical training at all. The game also uses "Hexerei" as a team-bonus label for characters tied to the circle.

In universe: Hexenzirkel members are called witches or mages, but the label is loose. Alice, the founder, is a long-lived polymath with alchemy, astrology, engineering, magic and medicine among her skills. Barbeloth reads fate by astrology. Rhinedottir practises the Art of Khemia. Nicole is an angel who survived the fall of her kind. Octavia travels the Sea of Stars. Two members, Andersdotter and I. Ivanovna N., never had any magical or combat training.

81.content:
Witch's Homework (also: Witch's Homework quests, The Little Witch's Dictionary, Witch's Eve Rite Passive, Witch's Eve Rite): Witch's Homework is a system from Version 6.2 in which The Little Witch's Dictionary hands out tasks, made by the Hexenzirkel's mages, to friends of the Traveler. Finishing a character's task makes them a Hexerei character and unlocks a bonus Talent for them, the Witch's Eve Rite Passive. In story terms the "homework" is the witches' long-range preparation to help Mondstadt in a future time of need.

In universe: Alice, a Hexenzirkel mage, wrote the dictionary with other mages. The title is a disguise: it claims to explain the storybook "The Little Witch and the Undying Fire", but the two books are unrelated and the dictionary is really full of tasks tailored to individual readers. The item text says it was made by the witches and is "actually filled with homework tailored by the Hexenzirkel for each reader."

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): each Witch's Homework quest belongs to one character. The player must own that character and have them at level 70 or higher. Finishing it makes the character a Hexerei character and unlocks their Witch's Eve Rite Passive, which also changes some of their Talents and Constellations.

82.content:
Witch's Revelation (also: Witch's Revelation Passive, Revelations by Chance): Witch's Revelation is a system from Version 6.7 in which the fortune-teller Barbeloth's Witch's Revelation Case holds oracles for particular characters. Completing a character's Witch's Revelation quest unlocks an extra Talent, the Witch's Revelation Passive, and enhances some of their Talents and Constellations. It is the sequel in spirit to Witch's Homework: Barbeloth and Alice are again behind it.

In universe: Barbeloth, a powerful fortune teller, is running a small divination stand just outside the Court of Fontaine, and tells the Traveler that as a Descender from beyond the world the Traveler's own fate cannot be predicted by most fortune tellers, herself included. She recently glimpsed an omen, followed it and caught threads of fate and the faces of their owners, who are all people the Traveler knows.

Gameplay: Gameplay (not literal lore): each quest belongs to one character. The player must own that character at level 70 or higher. Finishing it unlocks the Witch's Revelation Passive and changes some Talents and Constellations. The Passive also lets the character enter the Radiance state under certain conditions.
